 View Comments Metro Weather Politics Sports Business Puzzles Rhode Island Globe Magazine Opinion Health care Arts Lifestyle Education Cambridge & Somerville Money, Power, Inequality Spotlight Technology Climate Cars Real Estate Events Adam Himmelsbach | Celtics beat writer's notebook Why did things get so icy between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown? I’ve covered their entire careers. Here’s my take.
 Print this Article 
 View Comments With the Celtics' Jayson Tatum keeping his cool, a frustrated Jaylen Brown reacts after drawing one of his four fouls in Tuesday's 123-101 loss to the Celtics in Philadelphia. Matt Slocum/AP Photo/Matt Slocum In case there was any remaining doubt about whether iciness remained between Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown, it was erased when Tatum gave Brown a tap on the chest before Tuesday’s game between the Celtics and 76ers, and Brown stared straight ahead as if Tatum were just a team employee holding a T-shirt cannon. 
 Amid the passive aggressiveness, silent treatment, and awkward interviews on the topic, one question has persisted: Why, exactly, don’t these guys seem to like each other anymore? 
 I covered both players for the entirety of their successful nine-year run as Celtics teammates. It has been well-chronicled that they were not close friends, due mostly to their differing lifestyles and interests. But they got along fine. 
 Brown always bristled when referred to as option 1B, even if that is basically what he was when Tatum, option 1A, was healthy. Tatum was disappointed that Brown won both conference finals and Finals MVP awards over him in 2024, but if he had a gripe, it was more with the voters, not his teammate.

Enter Email Sign Up But last year’s dynamics between the two were unlike anything either player had experienced during his Boston tenure, and the belief here is that it elicited jealousy on both sides. 
 Related : Inside the final days of Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum’s tenure as Celtics teammates Tatum, of course, missed much of the season as he rehabbed the Achilles injury he suffered in May 2025. He sat on the bench, or at home, and watched the Celtics’ machine plow forward without him, with Brown leading the way. The “MVP” chants that were Tatum’s soundtrack for so many years were now transferred to Brown, who showed he can, indeed, carry a team. 
 Tatum even acknowledged part of the reason he returned last season rather than sitting out the entire year was because the Celtics were having success and he wanted to take part in it. 
 It probably did not help matters that Brown called the one season without Tatum the favorite of his career. Brown insisted that was just a reference to Boston’s overachievement, but the optics were undeniable. Regardless, for Brown, life was good. 
 Then in March, Tatum came back, but his MVP chants did not. Now, he was standing on the court and witnessing the fans’ swooning over Brown from a different lens. Tatum was sitting out back-to-backs and showing understandable signs of rust while Brown continued to carry the team. 
 But Tatum did return to his spot as the last starter to be announced, a league-wide sign of respect for a team’s top player. His confidence began to return, and he was eager to come back this year fully healthy and ready. 
 Brown had his taste of the top, and now he was staring at the reality that despite everything he did last season, he would soon return to his role as Tatum’s sidekick. 
 In a way, after nearly a decade of successfully making this partnership work, both players wanted something the other had. And that appeared to create a cold front. 
 In recent weeks, Tatum has done more to stay above the fray and minimize the soap opera. In a press conference, he said he had no beef with Brown and wished the focus was on all that they accomplished. Then before Tuesday’s game, he initiated the peace offering. 
 Both gestures fit his conflict-averse and generally warm personality. But it is also true that this situation is probably easier for him because, in essence, he won. He is back in his starring role, back healthy, back getting the MVP chants. 
 As much as Brown says he is embracing his role with the 76ers, he made it clear he was hurt by the trade. He said he even threw his phone across the room when he found out. 
 Celtics president of basketball operations Brad Stevens has insisted he did not consult with Tatum before making the deal. But Brown has shown he does not believe that. When Tatum posted a clip from his mini-documentary in which he said he was stunned by the Brown trade, Brown posted an emoji underneath that suggested he was not being truthful. 
 After the Celtics routed the 76ers, 123-101, on Tuesday in Philadelphia, Brown greeted most of his former teammates near midcourt while Tatum completed a television interview. By the time that interview ended, Brown was gone, but the cloud remained. 
 The Celtics and 76ers will not meet again until Jan. 21, when Brown makes his return to TD Garden. Whether the Brown and Tatum dynamic was a friendship or simply a business partnership, perhaps the lengthy wait until they meet again will give this all time to thaw.
